topic: The Great Loop: Connecting Derivatives and Integrals
target_audience: Advanced High School Students / First-year University Students

sections.title: Introduction: The Mystery of the Runner
sections.content: Introduce the central question: If we know how fast someone is moving at every moment, can we find their total distance? Conversely, if we know their position, can we find their speed? This section establishes the 'Inverse' relationship using a relatable character.
sections.example: Meet 'Dash the Cheetah.' Dash is running on a track. We see a split-screen: one side shows his Speedometer (Velocity) and the other shows his GPS Tracker (Position). The goal is to show that these two displays are telling the same story from different perspectives.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Slope and Area
sections.content: Quickly recap the two pillars of Calculus. Derivative represents the 'Slope' (Rate of Change) at a point. Integral represents the 'Area Under the Curve' (Accumulation) over an interval. Use simple geometric shapes to reinforce this.
sections.example: Visualizing a constant speed graph (a horizontal line). The 'Slope' of a position line is the velocity. The 'Area' under the velocity rectangle is the total distance. Animation shows a rectangle filling up with color as the cheetah moves.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a 'Moving Area.' Define a function S(x) that calculates the area under a curve from a fixed start point to a variable end point 'x'. This is the mental bridge to the Fundamental Theorem.
sections.example: Graph of f(t) = 2t. As a vertical slider moves along the x-axis, the shaded area grows. We plot the value of this shaded area on a new graph, showing that the 'Area' itself forms a new curve (x^2).

sections.title: The Big Reveal: The Fundamental Theorem
sections.content: Demonstrate that the rate at which the 'Area' accumulates is exactly equal to the height of the original function. This identifies the derivative of an integral as the original function itself. This is the 'Undo' button of Calculus.
sections.example: Animation: Zoom in on a tiny sliver of area (dA). Show that dA is approximately 'height (f(x)) times width (dx)'. Therefore, dArea/dx = f(x). A mathematical 'gearing' mechanism illustrates how the derivative 'unwraps' the integral.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Mathematical Application
sections.content: Apply the relationship to calculate a definite integral using an anti-derivative. Show the logic: To find the area, find a function whose derivative is the curve, then calculate the change in that function.
sections.example: Problem: Find the area under v(t) = 3t^2 from 0 to 2. Step 1: Think 'What function gives 3t^2 when differentiated?' (t^3). Step 2: Calculate the change in t^3 from 0 to 2 (8 - 0 = 8). Visual: The Cheetah reaches the 8m mark exactly as the area under the curve reaches 8.

sections.title: Summary: The Calculus Circle
sections.content: Conclude by visualizing the cyclical nature of calculus. Differentiation goes 'down' from Position to Velocity; Integration goes 'up' from Velocity to Position. They are two sides of the same coin.
sections.example: A circular infographic showing 'Position' at the top and 'Velocity' at the bottom. Arrows labeled 'Derivative' point down, and arrows labeled 'Integral' point back up, forming a perfect, infinite loop.
